attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Isn't a chance in hell' is a firm, categorical forecast about the pre-revenue AI cohort, so it is scored. The proposition also carries a claim about VC motives and a 'not real companies' label, but neither can be tested as an outcome. The cohort scope is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'functional business' as self-sustaining without new outside funding fits the passage, which talks about independence from further funding. The plain reading is ordinary. Requiring terminal evidence for every member before the claim counts as supported is strict but follows from the categorical wording.

evidence.note: Shows Reka was pre-revenue when it raised money in June 2023, so it belongs to the cohort. That is evidence about the condition, not the outcome, so it is context, not support.
Reka's own disclosure names customers and a new $110M raise. It gives no evidence that customer income pays for operations, so it does not contradict the claim.
The CEO reports subscriber growth and a revenue run rate, but nothing shows the company could run without outside funding.
Company disclosure of a Chapter 11 filing aimed at a sale, made 2026-10-12. Shows distress but not a terminal shutdown, and covers only one cohort member.

reviews.rationale: This is a categorical forecast with no deadline. No qualifying startup is shown to run on customer income without outside funding, so the contradiction test is not met. Character.AI's bankruptcy is not terminal and covers one member of a cohort that isn't fully named, so the support test is not met either. The claim about VC motives can't be tested. With no conclusive event, the claim stays unscored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the post-SVB timing, the 'no revenue' status, the amounts, and the claim that the money came from hype with no thought for viability. The causal kind is right.

contract.note: Reading 'no revenue' as status at the funding date is fair, and the speaker's own phrasing supports it. Requiring evidence of investor motives before the causal part counts as supported follows the 'because' and 'without any consideration' wording.

evidence.note: The investor's law firm confirms the $150M Series A in March 2023, after SVB, which supports the financing part. It says nothing about why investors put money in.

WSJ reporting, published 2023-03-23, quotes the company saying it had no revenue at the time of the round. Supports the pre-revenue part and shows the AI hype climate, but does not show what drove investors.

a16z's announcement cites user engagement and the product's data flywheel, which weighs a little against 'without any consideration'. It is promotional and does not show what diligence was actually done.
The subscription launched in May 2023, after the round. Since 'no revenue' is read at the funding date, this does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The factual parts hold: a $150M round in March 2023, after SVB, while the company had no revenue (e1, e2). The causal part, that hype drove the money with no thought for viability, is neither shown nor disproved. There are no investor decision records, and a16z's promotional rationale does not settle what diligence happened. The contract needs both parts for support, so the claim is unresolved.
